 Exercise Interventions Linked to Heart Rate Variability Shifts in Youth with Obesity
 Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram 
 Structured exercise programs for children and adolescents with overweight or obesity were associated with statistically significant within-arm pre-to-post improvements across multiple time-domain and frequency-domain heart rate variability metrics, according to a systematic review and meta-analysis published in Frontiers in Public Health. The quantitative synthesis, led by researchers Kaiyang Wu and Huishan Song from the School of Sports Science at Harbin Normal University in China, pooled data from eleven intervention studies to characterize changes in cardiac autonomic regulation following supervised exercise. Across the included exercise arms, participants demonstrated notable average increases in markers reflecting parasympathetic modulation and overall autonomic variability, including high-frequency power, pNN50, SDNN, and RMSSD, alongside a concurrent reduction in the low-frequency to high-frequency ratio. However, the investigators emphasized that these observed alterations stem from single-group pre-post comparisons, meaning that while they reflect measurable shifts over the intervention period, they cannot isolate exercise training effects from concurrent maturation, dietary influences, or other time-dependent factors.
 Pediatric overweight and obesity represent pervasive global public health challenges, with international surveillance indicating that childhood excess adiposity frequently persists into adulthood and elevates long-term cardiometabolic risk. Cardiovascular complications often begin to develop long before overt clinical disease manifests, with excess childhood adiposity tied to elevated blood pressure, vascular dysfunction, and unfavorable alterations in cardiac structure and functional performance. Heart rate variability serves as a non-invasive index of cardiac autonomic regulation by capturing the balance between sympathetic and parasympathetic influences exerted upon the sinus node. In youth with obesity, autonomic impairment is widespread and typically marked by vagal withdrawal and sympathetic predominance. While regular exercise forms a cornerstone of non-pharmacological management for pediatric obesity, global physical activity records show that roughly 81 percent of adolescents aged 11 to 17 years fall short of the World Health Organization recommendation of at least 60 minutes of daily moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, creating an urgent need to evaluate how structured training impacts cardiac autonomic pathways.
 To investigate how specific training protocols alter autonomic function, the authors registered their protocol in the PROSPERO database under registration number CRD420251102937 and conducted systematic searches across PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science for peer-reviewed studies published in English through March 20, 2026. Eligible studies were restricted to randomized controlled trials, non-randomized controlled trials, and quasi-experimental interventions assessing planned exercise regimens in children and adolescents aged 6 to 18 years with overweight or obesity. The quantitative framework relied on standardized mean change scores, synthesized as Hedges’ g using random-effects DerSimonian-Laird models with 95 percent confidence intervals. Because primary trials rarely provided the standard deviation of change scores directly, the authors applied a consistent assumed correlation coefficient of r = 0.50, subsequently verifying robustness across alternative correlation values of 0.30 and 0.70. Control groups from controlled trials were excluded from the primary pooling to preserve multi-arm protocol comparisons and avoid heterogeneity across disparate non-exercise, lifestyle, and usual-care control designs, though they were retained for secondary between-group sensitivity analyses.
 The quantitative synthesis compiled data across eleven trials published between 1997 and 2026, comprising eight randomized controlled trials and three controlled or quasi-experimental studies conducted across China, Brazil, the United States, Tunisia, and Colombia. Interventions spanned durations from 6 to 24 weeks, weekly schedules between 2 and 6 sessions, and total training doses ranging from 24 to 80 sessions. Exercise modalities encompassed aerobic training, resistance training, and mixed or other regimens, including plyometrics and game-based activities. Several publications incorporated multiple independent exercise arms evaluating distinct training prescriptions, including two arms from Farah and colleagues, three from Hamila and colleagues, two from Su and colleagues, and two from Rodríguez-Triviño and colleagues. Across these distinct arms, the researchers extracted measurements for six established autonomic parameters: the root mean square of successive differences between adjacent normal RR intervals (RMSSD), the standard deviation of normal-to-normal RR intervals (SDNN), the proportion of adjacent RR intervals differing by more than 50 milliseconds (pNN50), high-frequency power (HF), low-frequency power (LF), and the ratio of low-frequency to high-frequency power (LF/HF).
 For time-domain metrics, the pooled primary analyses demonstrated uniform directional increases in autonomic variation following exercise exposure. RMSSD, which reflects short-term beat-to-beat variability driven primarily by vagal activity, was evaluated across 15 exercise-arm comparisons from 10 distinct studies. The pooled effect showed a significant increase, with a Hedges’ g of 0.357 (95% CI: 0.180 to 0.534; p < 0.001) alongside moderate between-arm statistical heterogeneity (I2 = 52.3%, p = 0.009). SDNN, an established marker of total autonomic variability encompassing both branches of the autonomic nervous system, was synthesized from 10 exercise comparisons across seven studies, yielding a significant positive effect size of Hedges’ g = 0.374 (95% CI: 0.107 to 0.640; p = 0.006) accompanied by substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 72.4%, p < 0.001). Similarly, the vagally mediated marker pNN50, extracted from eight comparisons across five trials, showed an overall positive within-arm change under the primary model, yielding a Hedges’ g of 0.525 (95% CI: 0.119 to 0.931; p = 0.011) with high heterogeneity (I2 = 81.7%, p < 0.001).
 The frequency-domain synthesis yielded marked changes in parasympathetic frequency bands alongside distinct divergence across other spectral indices. High-frequency power, assessed across 15 comparisons from 10 studies, exhibited the largest point estimate among all evaluated indices, producing a pooled within-arm Hedges’ g of 0.951 (95% CI: 0.557 to 1.345; p < 0.001) under substantial statistical heterogeneity (I2 = 86.9%, p < 0.001). Conversely, low-frequency power, synthesized from 14 comparisons across nine trials, showed no statistically significant change following exercise, producing an imprecise Hedges’ g of −0.161 (95% CI: −0.596 to 0.273; p = 0.467; I2 = 89.2%). The LF/HF ratio, pooled across 11 comparisons from seven studies, demonstrated a statistically significant reduction, with a summary Hedges’ g of −0.502 (95% CI: −0.782 to −0.222; p < 0.001; I2 = 72.4%). The investigators cautioned that although LF/HF decreased, it represents a ratio change rather than a direct, validated index of sympathovagal balance, given the physiological complexity of low-frequency components and their susceptibility to baroreflex and respiratory influences.
 Exploratory subgroup analyses stratified intervention arms across exercise modality, training intensity, weekly session frequency, session duration, and total program length, though no formal statistical tests for interaction were conducted. For RMSSD, significant within-arm gains appeared across both low-frequency (2 to 3 weekly sessions; g = 0.322) and high-frequency (4 or more weekly sessions; g = 0.448) regimens, as well as moderate-duration (40 to 59 minutes; g = 0.271) and long-duration (60 or more minutes; g = 0.566) sessions. Aerobic exercise arms showed consistent increases across RMSSD (g = 0.301), SDNN (g = 0.288), and HF (g = 1.136), while resistance training demonstrated statistically significant positive effect sizes for RMSSD (g = 1.161), SDNN (g = 0.554), pNN50 (g = 1.003), and HF (g = 2.972). Nonetheless, the authors highlighted that resistance training was evaluated by only a single comparison from Farinatti and colleagues, precluding conclusions about relative modality efficacy. When classified by intensity, moderate-intensity training produced significant changes in RMSSD (g = 0.525) and SDNN (g = 0.658), whereas high-intensity protocols generated significant gains in pNN50 (g = 0.864) and HF (g = 2.025).
 To rigorously probe the stability of the meta-analytic findings, the authors executed an extensive series of sensitivity checks, leave-one-out models, and post hoc analytical re-specifications. Conventional leave-one-arm-out analyses affirmed the stability of the primary DerSimonian-Laird model, preserving statistical significance across every sequential removal for RMSSD, SDNN, pNN50, HF, and LF/HF, while LF consistently remained non-significant. However, more conservative statistical models exposed noteworthy analytical sensitivity. When re-analyzed using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation with a modified Hartung-Knapp confidence interval, the 95 percent confidence interval for pNN50 widened and crossed zero (−0.134 to 1.263), and randomized-arm-only sensitivity models likewise crossed zero for pNN50 (−0.107 to 0.624) and SDNN. HF and LF/HF estimates also showed vulnerability to single-study jackknife exclusions and to the removal of post-exercise recovery data from Hamila and colleagues, demonstrating that certainty differs considerably across individual heart rate variability parameters.
 Publication bias and small-study diagnostics further illuminated the limits of the available evidence base, reflecting data gathered from relatively few independent trial sources. Funnel plot asymmetry tests revealed statistically significant test signals for pNN50 (Begg’s p = 0.026; Egger’s p = 0.032), HF (Begg’s p = 0.005; Egger’s p = 0.001), and LF/HF (Begg’s p = 0.006; Egger’s p = 0.006). Despite these asymmetry signals, non-parametric trim-and-fill procedures imputed zero missing studies for RMSSD, SDNN, pNN50, HF, and LF/HF, leaving observed effect estimates unchanged. For LF, trim-and-fill analysis imputed four missing studies, which inverted the point estimate from negative to positive (g = 0.330, 95% CI: −0.440 to 1.100) while remaining statistically non-significant. The investigators noted that because total comparisons ranged from 8 to 15 derived from only 5 to 10 independent publications, funnel-based asymmetry tests possessed limited diagnostic power and could not definitively confirm or refute the presence of publication bias.
 In their interpretation, the authors outlined biologically plausible mechanisms through which physical training might enhance autonomic tone, while noting that their meta-analysis did not perform mediation analyses to confirm specific physiological pathways. Exercise may improve cardiorespiratory fitness and relieve resting autonomic strain, shift autonomic control toward greater resting parasympathetic modulation, reduce adiposity-related systemic inflammation through skeletal muscle myokine secretion, and enhance peripheral vascular function and hemodynamic regulation. Nevertheless, crucial methodological constraints temper clinical translation. The reliance on within-arm pre-to-post changes cannot disentangle exercise effects from natural somatic maturation, dietary changes, or regression to the mean. Furthermore, included trials displayed marked heterogeneity in physiological recording settings, including varied participant postures, breathing control, recording durations, device technologies, and reporting units, with certain studies pooling raw absolute power, normalized units, and logarithmically transformed figures. Consequently, the authors conclude that while structured exercise shows promising associations with improved vagal modulation in youth with obesity, confirmatory randomized controlled trials with standardized autonomic protocols and direct prescription comparisons remain essential.
 Subject of Research: Heart rate variability adaptations following structured exercise interventions in youth with overweight or obesity
 Article Title: Heart rate variability changes following exercise interventions in children and adolescents with overweight or obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis
